prompt: Alcohols and amines are both classified 1°, 2° or 3°, but the two are counted differently. What is counted in each?
choices: Alcohol: carbons attached to the carbon bearing the OH. Amine: carbons attached to the nitrogen itself
Both count the carbons attached to the heteroatom
Both count the carbons attached to the atom next to the heteroatom
Alcohol: carbons attached to the oxygen. Amine: carbons attached to the carbon next to N
explanation: (CH₃)₃C–OH is a tertiary alcohol because the carbon holding the OH carries three other carbons — the oxygen itself still has only one. (CH₃)₃N is a tertiary amine because the nitrogen itself carries three carbons. Counting the oxygen's own attachments would make every alcohol primary.
teach: Oxygen and nitrogen part company here because their attachment counts already mean something else. An oxygen carrying two carbons is not a tertiary alcohol — it is an ether. Nitrogen has three slots free, so it takes the 1°/2°/3° label directly; oxygen has only two, so the label had to move one atom over onto the carbon.

prompt: A benzene ring attached to something is a phenyl group. What are benzyl and benzoyl?
choices: Benzyl is phenyl plus a CH₂; benzoyl is phenyl plus a C=O
Benzyl is phenyl plus a C=O; benzoyl is phenyl plus a CH₂
Benzyl and benzoyl are both other names for phenyl
Benzyl has two rings; benzoyl has three
explanation: Phenyl is C₆H₅– bonded directly. Benzyl is C₆H₅CH₂–, the ring plus one carbon. Benzoyl is C₆H₅CO–, the ring plus a carbonyl. Three similar words, three different groups, and swapping them changes the compound.
teach: Benzylic is the one that earns its keep: the benzylic position is the carbon NEXT TO the ring, and a cation, radical or anion there is unusually stable because the ring delocalizes it. That single fact drives a large amount of aromatic-side-chain reactivity.
